name: Lower eyelid fat transposition

lead: In lower eyelid fat transposition the surgeon repositions the bulging fat pads of the lower eyelid, instead of removing them, and spreads that fat over the infraorbital rim. The aim is to fill the tear trough hollow and smooth the transition from lid to cheek, giving a more rested, even under-eye contour.

It is a variant of lower blepharoplasty. Wikipedia describes the repositioning approach as redistributing fat along the rim to treat tear trough deformities, and notes it is separate from fat transfer, in which fat harvested elsewhere is injected.

paras: A surgeon performs it as part of lower eyelid surgery, either through an incision just under the lashes or an incision on the inner surface of the eyelid with no external scar. The choice depends on whether excess skin must also be addressed.

Reported issues after lower blepharoplasty include swelling and bruising, which usually settle over several weeks, and eyelid malposition, which may be reduced by canthopexy or canthoplasty. It is done by a qualified surgeon under a surgical consent process.

angle.text: Instead of discarding lower-lid fat, the surgeon uses it to fill the groove under the eye. People choose it for under-eye bags with a hollow below them.

lead: Lower eyelid fat transposition is a technique within lower blepharoplasty in which the orbital fat that causes lower-lid bulging is mobilised and redistributed along the infraorbital rim rather than excised. The stated aim is to smooth the lid-cheek transition and treat tear trough deformities while maintaining contour along the rim.[1]

Lower blepharoplasty has two main approaches: a transcutaneous incision below the lashes that allows skin removal, and a transconjunctival incision inside the lid that leaves no external scar and removes no skin, so extra procedures may be needed when skin laxity is present.[1]

Blepharoplasty has old roots: the Roman writer Celsus described a skin excision to relax the eyelids in De Medicina, and Karl Ferdinand von Gräfe coined the word blepharoplasty in 1818 for eyelid repairs after cancer surgery.[1]
infobox: Fat transfer (injection of fat harvested elsewhere)

paras: Fat removal and fat repositioning can both be done through either approach. In repositioning, the fat is mobilised and redistributed along the infraorbital rim to blend the eyelid into the cheek.[1] Fat transfer is a different technique in which fat harvested from another body area is injected to restore periorbital volume.[1]
Swelling and bruising usually resolve over several weeks. Eyelid malposition is a possible complication, and canthopexy or canthoplasty may reduce it.[1]
